Hey Emilia - I'm not a convert and I haven't been to Beit Daniel before, but I know they have a very well-organised conversion programme (the largest non-Orthodox one in Israel!) and I know people who have had a really good experience converting there. 

If you are interested in considering Masorti (Conservative) conversion, I know a number of people who have converted through Kehilat Sinai on Burgashov that also had a really amazing experience there - it is a lovely community with an awesome Rabbi. The Masorti movement in Israel is smaller than Reform, and generally their conversion programmes can sometimes be a bit more ad hoc - so you would need to speak with a Rabbi about when the next intake starts.  Masorti communities tend to be more Anglo-heavy than reform, but both movements tend to be left-leaning. Religiously, Masorti and Reform just have different styles and different ways of encountering the Jewish tradition, and so I would recommend exploring both types of synagogues.

Before starting a conversion process with anyone, I'd recommend going along to a couple of services - get a feel for a place, see what they have to offer, see whether you like their vibe, and maybe arrange to meet with their rabbi (it makes sense before making a decision as intense and as life-altering as changing your religion!) :) If you haven't been to a synagogue service before, usually Kabbalat Shabbat services are the nicest and most accessible for newcomers. I would note that things are about to get very hectic for all synagogues and rabbis with the upcoming High Holidays, so it could be a good idea to either message very soon or wait until after the holidays are over. For non-Orthodox conversions in Israel generally, you don't need to have an A5 visa for a year - just an A5 visa. 

Lastly, we have an article about conversion to Judaism on our website which discusses the process in some general detail and some things to consider :) https://aic.org.il/conversion-to-judaism-in-israel-a-practical-overview-for-mixed-couples/
